title: Consumer Credit Act 1974: regulated agreements and improperly-executed agreements
principle: A credit hire agreement that provides credit to an individual is a regulated consumer credit agreement unless exempt; a regulated agreement that is not properly executed (s.61 form, prescribed terms, signature) is enforceable against the hirer only on an order of the court (s.65), and for agreements made before 6 April 2007 a missing prescribed term made it irredeemably unenforceable (old s.127(3), the Dimond v Lovell outcome). CCGUK avoids regulated status altogether by drafting the hire agreement to meet the RAO art 60F exemption.
text: s.65(1): "An improperly-executed regulated agreement is enforceable against the debtor or hirer on an order of the court only."

citation: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001 (SI 2001/544), art 60F
title: RAO 2001 art 60F: exempt agreements relating to the number of repayments
principle: A borrower-lender-supplier agreement for fixed-sum credit is an exempt (unregulated) credit agreement if the number of payments to be made by the borrower is not more than twelve, those payments are required within twelve months or less beginning with the date of the agreement, and the credit is provided without interest or other charges (art 60F(2)). CCGUK's credit hire agreement must therefore defer the hire charge for no more than 12 months, in no more than 12 payments, with no interest, fees or charges, so that the Consumer Credit Act regime (and the Dimond risk) does not apply.

citation: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, regs 29 and 30
title: CCRs 2013 regs 29-30: right to cancel and the normal 14-day cancellation period
principle: A consumer may cancel a distance or off-premises contract at any time in the cancellation period without giving a reason and without liability except as provided by the Regulations (reg 29); for a service contract the normal cancellation period ends 14 days after the day the contract is entered into (reg 30). The credit hire agreement is an off-premises service contract when signed at the client's home or roadside, so the 14-day clock starts on signature.

citation: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, reg 31
title: CCRs 2013 reg 31: cancellation period extended for breach of the information requirement
principle: If the trader fails to give the consumer the information on the right to cancel required by Schedule 2 paragraph (l), the cancellation period is extended by up to 12 months after the day it would otherwise have ended; if the information is given late within that 12 months, the period ends 14 days after the consumer receives it. For CCGUK this is the W v Veolia risk in modern form: a missing cancellation notice keeps the hire cancellable for over a year.

citation: Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, reg 36
title: CCRs 2013 reg 36: supply of a service during the cancellation period and the express request
principle: A trader must not start supplying the service before the end of the cancellation period unless the consumer has made an express request, which for an off-premises contract must be on a durable medium (reg 36(1)); if the consumer then cancels, they pay a proportionate amount for the service supplied up to cancellation (reg 36(4)); but the consumer bears no cost at all for the service supplied in the cancellation period if the trader failed to give the Schedule 2 paragraph (l) cancellation information or the information about that cost (reg 36(6)). This is why CCGUK's hire cannot start without a signed express request and the cancellation information: without them the whole hire charge for the first fortnight (or longer, under reg 31) is irrecoverable.

title: County Courts Act 1984 s.69: power to award interest on debts and damages
principle: In county court proceedings for a debt or damages the court may include simple interest, at such rate as it thinks fit or as may be prescribed, on all or part of the sum for all or part of the period between the cause of action arising and judgment (or earlier payment); interest may run at different rates for different periods and is not awarded where interest already runs on the debt. CCGUK's schedule of loss claims s.69 interest on hire, storage and recovery charges from the date each fell due; the rate is for the court (commonly a few per cent above base for commercial-type losses), and this is distinct from the ICOBS base + 4% benchmark.
text: s.69(1) (per snippet): in proceedings before the county court for the recovery of a debt or damages there may be included in any sum for which judgment is given simple interest, at such rate as the court thinks fit or as may be prescribed, on all or any part of the debt or damages.

citation: Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998, ss.1-6 and 5A; Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Rate of Interest) (No. 3) Order 2002 (SI 2002/1675)

principle: It is an implied term of a contract for the supply of goods or services between businesses that any qualifying debt carries simple statutory interest, currently 8% over the Bank of England base rate, from the day after the relevant day, plus a fixed-sum compensation of £40, £70 or £100 per debt depending on its size (s.5A). title: Road Traffic Act 1988 s.143: users of motor vehicles to be insured against third-party risks
principle: A person must not use, or cause or permit another to use, a motor vehicle on a road unless a policy of insurance (or security) covering third-party risks is in force for that use; contravention is an offence, with a defence for an employee driving in the course of employment who neither knew nor had reason to believe there was no cover. title: Road Traffic Act 1988 s.151: duty of insurers to satisfy judgments against persons insured or not insured by the policy
principle: Once a policy has been issued, the insurer must pay the person entitled to the benefit of a judgment for a liability that was required to be covered under s.145, even if the insurer would be entitled to avoid or cancel the policy and even where the driver was not insured under it (subject to exclusions and the property-damage cap in s.151(6)); the insurer can then recover from the insured or the person who caused or permitted the use. CCGUK uses s.151 to maintain leverage against an insurer that purports to void a policy: the third-party claimant's judgment must still be satisfied.

title: Road Traffic Act 1988 s.172: duty to give information as to the identity of the driver, and the reasonable-diligence defence
principle: Where a driver is alleged to have committed a relevant offence, the keeper must give such information as to the identity of the driver as the police may require, and any other person must give information in his power to give; failure is an offence (6 points) unless the keeper shows he did not know and could not with reasonable diligence have ascertained who the driver was (s.172(4)). title: Limitation Act 1980: six years for tort and contract, three years for personal injury
principle: An action founded on tort (s.2) or simple contract (s.5) must be brought within six years of the cause of action accruing; an action for damages for personal injuries must be brought within three years of the injury or the claimant's date of knowledge (s.11). CCGUK's limitation clock runs six years from the accident for vehicle damage, hire, storage and recovery claims and six years from breach for contractual claims against clients or suppliers; any injury element (three years) is referred out and not handled in-house.

title: Insurance Act 2015: duty of fair presentation and insurer remedies (non-consumer insurance)
principle: Before a non-consumer contract of insurance (such as CCGUK's fleet, hire and PHV policies) is entered into, the insured must make a fair presentation of the risk: disclose every material circumstance it knows or ought to know, or enough to put a prudent insurer on enquiry, in a reasonably clear and accessible manner (ss.3-5). The insurer has a remedy only if it shows that but for the breach it would not have written the risk or would have done so on different terms (s.8); Schedule 1 allows avoidance and retention of premium for a deliberate or reckless breach, otherwise a proportionate remedy (e.g. a claim reduced in proportion to the premium that would have been charged). CCGUK must disclose the true uses of each fleet unit (credit hire, self-drive, PHV) and its claims history, or risk a voided fleet policy.

citation: Consumer Insurance (Disclosure and Representations) Act 2012, ss.2-5 and Schedule 1
title: Consumer Insurance (Disclosure and Representations) Act 2012: consumer misrepresentation and insurer remedies
principle: A consumer's pre-contract duty is to take reasonable care not to make a misrepresentation to the insurer (s.2); the insurer has a remedy only for a 'qualifying misrepresentation' made in breach of that duty (s.4), and the remedy depends on the consumer's state of mind (s.5, Sch 1): deliberate or reckless misrepresentation allows avoidance, refusal of all claims and retention of premium (unless unfair), whereas a careless misrepresentation gives only a proportionate remedy based on what the insurer would have done had it known the truth. CCGUK uses it when a client's own insurer avoids or voids a policy: challenge the characterisation of carelessness as deliberate, and push for cancellation rather than avoidance ab initio.

citation: Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 2012, ss.56-60
title: LASPO 2012 ss.56-60: ban on referral fees in personal injury claims
principle: Regulated persons (solicitors, barristers, claims management companies and, by regulations, insurers) may not pay or receive referral fees for personal injury or death claims (s.56), and the ban cannot be avoided by dressing the payment up as a fee for referring a connected claim such as credit hire or vehicle damage arising from the same accident; regulators must monitor and enforce the ban (ss.57-59) and s.60 defines regulated persons. CCGUK therefore refers injury elements out without any fee in either direction and keeps credit hire referrals free of any payment linked to an injury claim.

citation: Legal Services Act 2007, s.12 and Schedule 2
title: Legal Services Act 2007 s.12 and Sch 2: reserved legal activities (rights of audience and conduct of litigation)
principle: Reserved legal activities are the exercise of a right of audience, the conduct of litigation, reserved instrument activities, probate activities, notarial activities and the administration of oaths (s.12(1)); Schedule 2 defines the conduct of litigation as issuing proceedings, their commencement, prosecution and defence, and ancillary functions, and a right of audience as the right to appear before and address a court including calling and examining witnesses. Carrying on a reserved activity without authorisation is an offence (s.14). CCGUK is not authorised, so litigation documents are prepared as drafts for the claimant as litigant in person or an instructed solicitor to sign and file; pre-action correspondence is not reserved, and lay representation in small claims is separately permitted.
text: Sch 2 para 4(1) (per snippet): the "conduct of litigation" means (a) the issuing of proceedings before any court in England and Wales, (b) the commencement, prosecution and defence of such proceedings, and (c) the performance of any ancillary functions in relation to such proceedings (such as entering appearances to actions).

citation: Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, s.19 (with ss.23 and 26-27)
title: FSMA 2000 s.19: the general prohibition on carrying on regulated activities without authorisation
principle: No person may carry on, or purport to carry on, a regulated activity in the United Kingdom unless authorised or exempt; breach is a criminal offence (s.23) and agreements made in the course of an unauthorised regulated activity are unenforceable against the other party (ss.26-27). Regulated claims management activity (RAO arts 89G onwards) covers personal injury and financial-product claims; vehicle-damage and credit hire recovery is generally understood to fall outside it, but CCGUK must stop and check the perimeter (PERG 2.7) whenever injury or a complaint against an FCA-regulated firm about a financial product is involved.

title: Fraud Act 2006 ss.1-4: fraud by false representation, failing to disclose and abuse of position
principle: Fraud (s.1) is committed by dishonestly making a false representation (s.2), dishonestly failing to disclose information one is under a legal duty to disclose (s.3), or dishonestly abusing a position of trust (s.4), in each case intending to make a gain or cause loss or expose another to a risk of loss; no actual gain or loss is required. For CCGUK this is the criminal perimeter around every claim: inflated heads, invented hire days, adopted or constructed accounts and false statements in forms are s.2 fraud for the client and for anyone who constructs the account.
text: s.2(1): "A person is in breach of this section if he (a) dishonestly makes a false representation, and (b) intends, by making the representation (i) to make a gain for himself or another, or (ii) to cause loss to another or to expose another to a risk of loss."

citation: Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015, s.57
title: Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015 s.57: dismissal of personal injury claims for fundamental dishonesty
principle: Where a claimant would otherwise be entitled to damages for personal injury but the court finds on the balance of probabilities, on the defendant's application, that the claimant has been fundamentally dishonest in relation to the primary claim or a related claim, the court must dismiss the whole claim including the honest parts, unless the claimant would suffer substantial injustice; a 'related claim' includes a credit hire or vehicle damage claim brought in the same proceedings. Although CCGUK refers injury out, a dishonest hire claim run alongside a client's injury claim can sink the injury claim and expose CCGUK to non-party costs (Kindertons v Murtagh).

title: UK GDPR Art 5: principles relating to processing of personal data
principle: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently; collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes; adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary; accurate and kept up to date, with inaccurate data erased or rectified without delay (Art 5(1)(d)); kept no longer than necessary; and processed securely; the controller is accountable for demonstrating compliance (Art 5(2)). CCGUK's DSAR and credit-file work leans on Art 5(1)(d) accuracy, and its own file hygiene (minimisation, retention schedule, hashes) is the Art 5 compliance story.

citation: Data Protection Act 2018, s.10 and Schedule 1 (Parts 2-4)
title: Data Protection Act 2018 Sch 1: conditions for special category and criminal-offence data, and the appropriate policy document
principle: Schedule 1 supplies the domestic conditions required by UK GDPR Arts 9 and 10: Part 2 substantial-public-interest conditions (for example preventing fraud, para 14, and insurance, para 20), Part 3 additional conditions for criminal convictions data (including consent and processing necessary for legal claims, para 33), and Part 4 the requirement for an appropriate policy document and additional safeguards that attaches to most Part 1 and Part 2 conditions. Driving convictions, penalty points and NIPs are criminal offence data: CCGUK should identify the specific condition it relies on for each processing (legal claims, para 33, for client and third-party driver data; an insurance or fraud-prevention condition where applicable) and, because the brief and ICO guidance call for it, keep an appropriate policy document and retention schedule in any event, even where the particular Part 3 condition may not strictly require one.

citation: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c. 18), including s.103 and Schedule 10 (data subject complaints)
title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025: reforms to UK GDPR and DPA 2018, including the duty to handle data subject complaints
principle: The 2025 Act amends the UK GDPR and DPA 2018 (recognised legitimate interests, DSAR 'reasonable and proportionate' search and clock-stopping, automated decision-making, ICO restructuring and more) and, through s.103 and Schedule 10, requires controllers to facilitate complaints from data subjects, acknowledge them within 30 days and respond without undue delay, with the ICO able to expect that the controller's process has been used before it takes up a complaint. Per the blueprint, the core Part 5 reforms commenced on 5 February 2026 (SI 2026/82) and the complaints provisions on 19 June 2026; CCGUK must have a documented data-protection complaints process and should expect insurers to insist on their own process before an ICO complaint.

citation: Private Hire Vehicles (London) Act 1998, ss.2, 6, 7 and 12
title: Private Hire Vehicles (London) Act 1998: operator, vehicle and driver licensing in London
principle: In London no one may accept or make provision for private hire bookings without a PHV operator's licence (s.2); no vehicle may be used as a private hire vehicle on a road without a PHV licence for that vehicle (s.6), which TfL grants only if the vehicle is suitable, safe, comfortable, in good condition and properly insured, subject to conditions (s.7); and no one may drive a PHV without a PHV driver's licence (s.12). citation: FSMA 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001, SI 2001/544, arts 89G–89M (inserted by SI 2018/1253)
title: Specified claims management activities and the kinds of claim they cover
principle: Art 89G: seeking out, referrals and identification of claims or potential claims (seeking out persons who may have a claim; referring details of a claim/claimant to another person; identifying a claim or claimant) when carried on in relation to a personal injury, financial services or financial product, housing disrepair, specified benefit, criminal injury or employment-related claim. Arts 89H–89M: advising a claimant, investigating a claim or representing a claimant in relation to each of those six kinds respectively (89H personal injury; 89I financial services/product; 89J housing disrepair; 89K specified benefit; 89L criminal injury; 89M employment-related). "Personal injury claim" takes the CPR meaning (damages for or arising from personal injuries). Exclusions follow in arts 89N–89W (e.g. legal professionals, charities, persons with insurance-distribution permissions acting in relation to a contract of insurance).

citation: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (Commencement No. 6 and Transitional and Saving Provisions) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/82
title: DUAA 2025 commencement: core data protection reforms 5 February 2026; data subject complaints duty (s.103, Sch 10 — new DPA 2018 s.164A) 19 June 2026
